newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end mixed in choppy trade.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end mixed in choppy trade.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended mostly lower Tuesday, except for palladium which closed sharply higher, but volumes were light and activity was driven by year-end book squaring, traders said.
COMEX and NYMEX will close Wednesday for the New Year holiday.

"Gold didn't do much, but after yesterday's weakness in silver, more stops were triggered below the $4.80 level (basis March)," North American Equity Services floor trader John Geraghty said. "Palladium jumped on some fund buying, but volumes were light across the board," he said.
COMEX February gold ended down $2.00 an ounce at $369.20, not far from the contract low at $367.70, but was driven by last minute position squaring on total estimated volume of 6,000 lots.
Spot gold in the bullion market ended quoted $367.45/367.95, compared to the London Tuesday morning fix at $369.55, and the New York close Monday at $369.25/75.
There was no Tuesday afternoon gold fix in London due to the market's early close for the New Year holiday.
March silver ended down 2.5 cents at $4.790, after recovering from a session low at $4.710.
Silver fixed sharply lower in London Tuesday morning at $4.7975 an ounce, following the fall on COMEX Monday afternoon.
But the spot gold/silver ratio ended little changed at 77.03, after recovering from a three month low at 75.50 lastd Friday.
Spot gold closed the year not far above the three year lows at $366.00 seen in late November, after retreating steadily all year from five year highs at $417.00 an ounce seen in February.
"Gold has far more bear points against it than it does bull ones," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said.
A further 1,000 tonnes of gold could be sold by central banks in 1997, while mine supply is slowly increasing, despite the decline in South African production, he said.

On the demand side, physical demand remains soft, with CRU International reporting shipments of gold bullion into the bid six import markets of Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Dubai and Turkey down 13 percent in the first 10 months of 1996.
NYMEX March palladium ended up $5.25 an ounce at $124.25, after seeing a session high at $124.70, the highest level since November 13 for the March contract.
The March/June palladium spread ended at a premium of 25 cents an ounce, up from the more normal contango of $1.25 an ounce, the last time both contracts traded on December 27.

"Palladium has been looking the strongest contract in the complex for some time now, with substitution into palladium from platinum in industrial processes increasing steadily," CPM Group analyst Ted Kempf said.
"Plus the Russian contract talks were delayed because of Russian fiscal problems, leaving some participants unsure of their allocations."
NYMEX April platinum closed down $1.30 an ounce at $374.50, with the April platinum/gold spread rising to $3.50 an ounce from $2.50 an ounce Tuesday.
Platinum "production is rising steadily in southern Africa, while scrap recovery in the West continues to rise," Arnold said.
"The Russians continue to sell in whatever volumes they think the market will bear and give Moscow a reasonable return in foreign exchange earnings," he said.
Meanwhile, "Japanese offtake is falling under the impact of a depreciating yen, while the autocatalyst market can best be described as mature," Arnold said.
